title: The Unfolded Protein Response and Bile Acid Metabolism
text:
Cholestatic liver diseases are common hepatic disorders where liver bile acid levels can
increase and lead to cirrhosis and liver failure. There are few effective medical therapies and no
cures for these diseases, We investigate a protective mechanism in the liver termed the XBP1
pathway and how it regulates bile acid metabolism.

title: Engineering exosomes for new gRNA/Cas therapeutics to  eliminate HBV infection
text:
Patients with HBV infection are subject to prolonged (often lifelong) treatment due to the lack of curative therapeutics.
Thus, multimodal, robust therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to eliminate HBV cccDNA, which sustains viral
replication and is refractory to the current antiviral regimens. Recently, we have designed and selected specific and
potent gRNA/Cas9 HBV gene-editing drugs using HBV cellular models. We have also developed an exosome-based
drug delivery system packaged with these synthetic gRNA/Cas9 HBV gene-editing drugs to specifically target human
hepatocytes. In this proposal, we will evaluate the antiviral efficacy and any potential off-target effects of a novel
gRNA/Cas9/Cas12/Cas13-based gene-editing regimen targeting HBV DNA and RNA, both in vitro and in vivo. The
objective of this project is to lay the foundation for future clinical studies, to achieve our long-term goal of curing
chronic HBV infection. If successful, this novel drug design and delivery platform may be utilized to combat existing
and emerging viral diseases. It is thus clinically significant, timely, and relevant to public health.

title: The (onto)genetic basis of phenotypic integration
text:
This project will investigate the molecular, genetic, and developmental mechanisms through which multiple traits
can become linked and manifest together as a complex phenotype. A wide array of phenotypes, including most
diseases, are made up of multiple sub-phenotypes (e.g. symptoms) connected by a common underlying
molecular or genetic basis. The results of this work will illuminate the specific mechanisms through which such
phenotypes arise, contributing to our understanding of how differences between individuals and across species
are formed, and will advance a new animal model for studies of this nature.

title: Molecular Mechanism of Rnd3 Regulation in Lung Cancer
text: Summary for Project 4 led by Research Project Leader Katie Ryan, PhD Lung cancer is one of the most common cancer types and claims the lives of more Arkansans than any other cancer. Most lung cancers metastasize, which leads to poor prognosis. Studying mechanisms that drive metastatic potential is key to unlocking new strategies for the treatment of this deadly form of cancer. The major goal of this COBRE Research Project is to investigate the role of a non-canonical Rho GTPase, Rnd3, as a mediator of lung cancer metastasis. Rnd3 has been proposed as an independent marker for lung cancer-related survival. Our data show patients with lung adenocarcinoma expressing low levels of Rnd3 have significantly higher survival probability rates compared to those with high levels of Rnd3. Yet, the impact of Rnd3 on the molecular features of lung cancer remain obscure. We found that suppressing Rnd3 expression in lung adenocarcinoma cells decreased cell migration and invasion, two hallmarks of metastasis. We then made the exciting discovery that Rnd3 regulation of both cell migration and invasion occurs independently of ROCK1 signaling, one of the best-studied regulators of Rnd3 activity. Our findings support the idea that Rnd3 is regulated by a novel pathway in lung cancer. Rnd3 is not regulated by the canonical Rho GTPase cycle. Rather, this non- canonical GTPase is regulated at the transcriptional level and by post-translational modifications (PTMs) that affect Rnd3 localization, stability, and protein–protein interactions. The molecular features of Rnd3 regulation are understudied and not well defined. The central hypothesis for this COBRE project is that Rnd3 regulation in lung cancer occurs through a ROCK1-independent mechanism that alters both the phosphorylation status and localization of Rnd3, resulting in increased metastatic potential in vitro and in vivo. To test this hypothesis, we will pursue the following Specific Aims: (Aim 1) elucidate ROCK1-independent regulation of Rnd3 in lung cancer, (Aim 2) delineate the roles of PTMs as determinants of Rnd3 function in lung cancer, and (Aim 3) investigate in vivo the role of Rnd3 in mediating lung cancer metastasis. The proposed work is significant because lung cancer is the major cause of cancer death in the US, and metastasis is a key driver of this outcome. The proposed research aligns with the scientific theme of the Center for Molecular Interactions in Cancer (CMIC). The COBRE support will help establish my independent research program by providing mentoring and access to Research Cores that are critical to identifying the molecular basis of Rnd3-mediated control of metastatic potential in lung cancer.

title: Integrated Therapies for Alcohol use in Alcohol-associated Liver Disease (ITAALD) - Virginia Commonwealth University
text: Alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) has high morbidity and mortality but no FDA-approved therapy. Patients with AH rarely have their underlying alcohol use disorder (AUD) concomitantly addressed. The Integrated Therapies for Alcohol-associated Liver Disease (ITAALD) trial tests the efficacy of an integrated therapeutic strategy with combined treatments for AH and AUD in patients with severe AH.

title: Dopamine Availability and Developmental Pathways of Adolescent Depression and Anhedonia
text:
Depression begins in adolescence, occurs at high rates, and is related to impaired functioning and suicide.
Understanding the mechanisms of depression in the developing brain will improve our ability to prevent and
treat this pernicious disorder. To investigate the role of the dopamine system, which is altered in depression
and contributes to many features of depression, we will measure brain structure and function, dopamine
function, inflammation, reward-driven behavior, and smartphone-based real-life experience and behavior,
contributing to understanding how depression develops across adolescence and young adulthood.

title: PamON: 3D imaging of live and incubated engineered tissue with photoacoustic microscopy
text:
The research proposed in this project will result in PamON, a first-of-kind integrated platform for non-destructive
imaging of Tissue Engineered Medical Products (TEMPS), driven by non-invasive, non-contact photoacoustic
signal detection and longitudinal volumetric imaging. PamON will rapidly advance the ability to image 3D tissues
and their constitutive biological re-structuring under precisely controlled physio-chemical conditions, beyond
what is possible with traditional optical microscopy. In the long-term, it will advance regenerative and reparative
approaches to benefit Human patients, with broader impacts in all areas of Tissue Engineering.

title: Structure and Function of the Conoid in Toxoplasma
text:
The goal of our project is to develop a comprehensive understanding of unique structural
features that form the internal skeleton of apicomplexan parasites that cause serious human
diseases. The insights gained from this project may inform future efforts to develop improved
treatments for parasitic diseases.

title: Dynamic Cell-Matrix Interactions Dictate Thoracic Aortopathy
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – CORE B: SCIENTIFIC Altered cell signaling and gene expression secondary to predisposing genetic variants in thoracic aortopathy and related risk factors such as hypertension ultimately control the composition, structure, and function of the aorta that dictates its biomechanical properties and thus its potential vulnerability to aneurysmal dilatation, dissection, and rupture. There is, therefore, a pressing need to quantify the biomechanical phenotype of the diseased aorta and to relate it to its transcriptional profile. This biomechanical quantification must be multiaxial because of the complex loads experienced by the ascending aorta over a cardiac cycle. Core B will use unique, computer- controlled, multiaxial experimental devices for data collection and unique machine learning for data synthesis. Specifically, this Scientific Core will provide consistent biomechanical testing and computational modeling across all Projects that study mouse models of thoracic aortopathy, thus generating an essential data base from which general (rather than mouse-specific or lab-specific) conclusions can be inferred from an objective method for integrating data. In particular, we will use 2 validated multi-modality computer-controlled biomechanical testing devices to consistently quantify key geometric and mechanical metrics across all key mouse models used in Projects 1-4, testing equal numbers of male and female mice to study sex as a biological variable and testing young and older mice to study age as a biological variable. Importantly, computer-control of the testing protocols significantly increases reproducibility and rigor. For consistency, we will similarly test human aortic samples (from Project 2) using another device but the same cyclic biaxial testing protocols and the same nonlinear constitutive relation for quantification. Given the expected large, unique database in mice, we will also extend our new deep learning “constitutive artificial neural network” (CANN) to correlate the biomechanical phenotype and transcriptional profile in the mouse models, focusing initially on the top ~ 50 up- or down-regulated genes across Projects that relate to the mechano-biological axis: actomyosin, cell-matrix interactions, and matrix. Our recent work connecting biomechanics with 14 key measures of histology support this machine learning approach. This Scientific Core is significant for it will address a pressing unmet need for consistent multiaxial histological and biomechanical findings across diverse mouse models of thoracic aortopathy that can be correlated with biological findings as well as human data and it is innovative for it will enable a unique integrative analysis of a large data set (using a CANN) that promises to uncover true genotype – phenotype relationships for diseased aortas, based both on measured biaxial biomechanical changes and associated transcriptional changes.

title: Leveraging linked registry and electronic health records to examine long-term patient outcomes after peripheral vascular intervention"
text:
The proposed research will evaluate long-term patient outcomes after peripheral vascular interventions for
peripheral arterial disease and assess heterogeneity of treatment effect. These will be supported by
implementing and advancing data linkage, natural language processing, and effect modifier assessment
methods for vascular research. The proposed research is relevant to NIH's mission to foster fundamental
knowledge generation and innovative research strategies that will ultimately help protect and improve health.

title: Dual Targeting of PIM and JAK for ATL therapy
text:
This application will explore combination therapy co-targeting the PIM and JAK signaling pathways in HTLV-I
transformed ATL cells. These studies will lead to the identification of more effective therapies for the treatment
of ATL diseases.

title: Development of Inhibitors Against SARS CoV-2 NSP16 Methyltransferase
text:
The currently ongoing pandemic of coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19) is posing a severe infectious threat to
human population across the globe, with more than 6.8 million deaths occur due to SARS-CoV-2 since its
emergence in 2019 in Wuhan. Since many viruses have pandemic potential, broad-spectrum antivirals are
urgently needed. Our proposed drug discovery research is of great potential in creating new broad-spectrum
therapeutic agents to combat these disastrous viral infections.

title: Enhancing sensitivity to GNAQ/11 pathway inhibitors by antagonizing the serotonin HTR2B receptor in uveal melanoma
text:
Uveal melanoma, also termed ocular melanoma, is the most common adult eye cancer, and it often results
in untreatable metastasis to the liver. More than 90% of uveal melanoma patients contain activating
mutations in GNAQ or GNA11, and these mutant GNAQ/11 inappropriately and continually promote uveal
melanoma cell proliferation and tumor growth. There is an urgent need to develop treatments for uveal
melanoma, and this project will investigate the idea that select G protein-coupled receptors can be inhibited
to thereby induce a less active and more easily inhibited state of mutant GNAQ/11

title: Cardiovasology
text: The “Cardiovasology” Training Program at Mayo Clinic is an avenue for advanced training of the specialized workforce of physicians/scientists focused on heart health and disease, with a focus on heart failure. This proposal expands Program faculty and scope, deepens and broadens its scientific expertise, fosters excellence of mentors and trainees, and integrates new training in emerging technologies and innovations. This Program builds on over four-decades of success in attracting, mentoring and retaining talented individuals that will form the next generation of science leaders and scholars in this country.

title: Mass Spectrometry-Based Protein Footprinting: A New Tool for Amyloid Protein Aggregation
text:
The lack of cures and prevention of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) stems in part from an incomplete understanding
of the aggregation of plaque-forming Amyloid beta protein, and by the role of another protein, ApoE, a biomarker
of AD. We seek to understand these proteins in vitro and in reprogrammed neurons from individuals who have
AD.

title: Development and Validation of a Genomic Surveillance Workflow for Antimicrobial Resistance in Aquaculture Pathogens
text:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in aquaculture threatens animal health, food production, and environmental
ecosystems, with potential impacts on human health through the food supply and shared microbial environments.
This project will identify how resistance develops and spreads in important aquaculture bacteria and will create
tools to detect resistance earlier and more efficiently. These efforts will support improved monitoring and
antimicrobial stewardship, helping to reduce the spread of resistant bacteria across animal, environmental, and
human health systems.

title: Endolysosomal Physiology of Myeloid Phagocytes
text:
This research investigates how specialized proteins called ion channels control the internal machinery of immune
cells that protect us from infections and maintain healthy tissues. By understanding how these channels work in
immune cells throughout the body - from brain to liver to lungs - we aim to develop new ways to boost the immune
system's ability to fight infections and remove harmful debris from tissues. This knowledge could lead to better
treatments for a range of diseases, including viral infections, chronic inflammatory conditions, and cancer, where
the cleaning and recycling functions of immune cells are not working properly.

title: Developing the Next Generation of Genome-Editing Tools for Large Cargo DNA Integration
text:
Our lab studies CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs), RNA-guided integrases that enable site-specific DNA
insertion without double-strand breaks. We aim to re-engineer CASTs using structural biology, high-throughput
screening, and machine learning to improve their activity, specificity, and utility in diverse organisms. Our long-
term vision is to develop a next-generation genome editing platform for precise therapeutic and synthetic biology
applications.

title: Non-human primate MHC and KIR Allele Discovery and Typing Technology Development
text: The program aims to enhance immunological and infectious disease research using nonhuman primate (NHP) models by providing detailed knowledge of NHP Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC), Killer-cell Immunoglobulin like Receptor (KIR), and Fc Receptor (FcR) genes, loci, and alleles. It also aims to develop genotyping technologies that are freely accessible to the NHP research community and provide all sequences generated to NIAID-designated, publicly available databases. The program also aims to develop and apply whole genome/whole exome sequencing (WGS) to the MHC, KIR, and FcR regions, and generate and make publicly available supplemental information, including primer and probe definitions and familial relationships of animals used in gene discovery and allele frequency studies. This information will support the development and interpretation of transplantation and other studies in the NHP pre-clinical model.

title: Molecular Biophysics of Mitochondrial Membranes
text:
The proposed research will investigate the molecular mechanisms involved in the generation, storage, and
conversion of energy within the cell's power plant, the mitochondrion. It will also aim to identify promising new
strategies for pharmacological control of mitochondria to treat metabolic disorders.
